opening.headline: We explain why our service collapses when the external model API becomes slow through the failure patterns of distributed systems, and distinguish which patterns are necessary for AI calls.
body: As the external model API slows down, threads waiting for calls pile up, all clients immediately retry failed calls, increasing the load, and eventually other functions unrelated to the model may become unresponsive. AI calls are not subject to any special failure laws. It suffers from the same typical distributed system problems that any call that crosses the network suffers from.

In this class, we first look at the Well-Architected principle, which is a lens for viewing reliability, and then look at Circuit Breaker, which prevents calls that will fail, Saga and compensation transactions, which reverse intermediate failures in multi-step operations, and queue-based load leveling and dead-letter queues, which absorb the load. At the end, we identify where to attach these patterns to the AI ​​call.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the operation of reliability patterns such as Circuit Breaker, Saga, compensation transaction, and queue-based load leveling
You can distinguish which patterns are needed at each point in the AI call.
Explains how exponential backoff, jitter, and count caps reduce retry flooding, and distinguishes between errors that are retryable and those that are not.

screens.title: When the external model slowed down, our service collapsed with it.
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow how the disorder spreads chronologically. As each stage progresses, the scope of the problem increases.

visual.alt: A timeline diagram showing delays, build-up of waits, bursts of retries, and cascading failures over time.

steps.title: 1. External model API is slow
steps.body: Model calls that normally take 2 seconds will now take 30 seconds. The request doesn't fail, it's just slowed down. This delay is typical of a temporary defect. Temporary resource shortages, network slowdowns, or timeouts usually correct themselves after a while.

steps.title: 2. Waiting for a call builds up
steps.body: While waiting for a call to complete, it holds up resources such as threads, memory, and connections. As requests continue to come in, waiting calls pile up and resources start to run out. Even if you set a timeout, it will take up the same resources until the period ends.

steps.title: 3. All clients retry immediately
steps.body: When thousands of clients resend failed calls simultaneously, the service trying to recover experiences a larger-than-normal load all at once. Retries are effective for transient faults, but they increase the load and slow recovery for persistent faults. The server can indicate when to try again by adding a Retry-After header to the 429 or 503 response, but a client that retries immediately is ignoring this standard signal.

steps.title: 4. Even functions unrelated to the model are stopped.
steps.body: Depleted resources are also used for functions other than model calls. Eventually, even functions such as customer inquiry or login will become unresponsive. It is a chain failure that follows a single failure.

steps.title: Questions for this class
steps.body: This situation is not a problem caused by AI. So the solution also lies within the already known patterns of distributed systems. In this class, we will explain which patterns block which points.

screens.outro: Now that we have seen how the disorder spreads, let us recall similar experiences.

items.prompt: AI services are also not free from the failure patterns of general distributed systems. Have you ever seen a similar situation?
items.answer: It is the same problem if the calling party also experiences slowdown when the payment service or database slows down. Model APIs are more prone to this problem due to their long response times and high volatility.

items.prompt: Where are we stuck when the services we rely on slow down?
items.answer: Most often, they are blocked on shared resources that multiple functions use together, such as thread pools, connection pools, and memory. If the sticking point is a shared resource, the path for problems in one function to spread to other functions is already open.

items.prompt: Did retry help or make things worse?
items.answer: Retries help for temporary faults, and worsen them for faults that last more than a few minutes. Distinguishing between the two cases is the key to this lesson. If you can't tell the difference, you'll have the false belief that the more retries you make, the more stable it becomes.

screens.outro: Now, let’s check through the Well-Architected principles how to view reliability.

screens.title: Well-Architected Principles: A Lens for Viewing Reliability
screens.lead: Select each tab to see the questions the five pillars ask for AI call design.

tabs.label: Overview
tabs.body: The Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework has separate perspectives for AI and ML workloads. We provide principles and recommendations tailored to AI and ML for each of the five pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Cost Optimization, and Performance Optimization. The pillars have to be interchanged, so raising one pillar to its maximum will weaken the other pillar.

tabs.label: operational excellence
tabs.body: To operate an AI system reliably, a solid model development foundation is required. Before you begin, the document recommends clarifying the problem to be solved and the outcomes needed, and breaking down the goals into measurable indicators. Code and documents are version managed using tools such as Git, and prompts for generative AI applications are also instructed to be developed and managed using tools. The question is, ‘What do we call success, and can we look back on what has changed?’

tabs.label: reliability
tabs.body: The question of the reliability pillar is 'Will the service continue to operate even if some parts fail?' Circuit Breaker, Compensatory Transaction, and Queue-Based Load Leveling that we will see in this class are all patterns that answer this question.

tabs.label: Cost Optimization and Performance Optimization
tabs.body: Retries increase the number and cost of calls, while queues stabilize throughput at the expense of increasing delays. A balanced design looks at how reliability-boosting devices impact cost and response time. The security pillar deals with what comes and goes and access rights.

screens.outro: Now that we have the lens in place, let's start with Circuit Breaker, which prevents calls from failing.

screens.title: Retry Principles: Exponential Backoff, Jitter, Retryable Errors
screens.lead: Move the slider to build up your retry policies layer by layer. At each stage, the explanation changes as to how the load changes when 1000 clients encounter the same failure. The latency numbers are assumed values ​​to demonstrate the concept.

visual.alt: When there is no jitter, retry requests are clustered into bars at the same time, and when there is jitter, the two bar graphs are evenly distributed across the time axis.
labels: Elapsed time in seconds since failure occurred
Number of retry requests that arrived at that time

stops.body: It is sent again as soon as it fails. Since the failure starts at the same time, 1000 clients fail at the same moment and resend at the same moment. Just as services are trying to recover, they are hit with requests that are several times their usual volume. This process of synchronizing the actions of clients at the same time is called synchronization, and is the main cause of excessive retry attempts.

Each time you fail, the waiting time is doubled. Assuming that you increase it to 1 second, 2 seconds, 4 seconds, or 8 seconds, the frequency of calls from the same client will decrease. However, clients that start at the same time wait at the same interval, so they still arrive together at the same time. In a simulation on the AWS Architecture Blog, backoff alone resulted in clusters of clients, leaving contention.

Jitter is adding randomness to latency. For example, if this wait cap is 4 seconds, it will not send at exactly 4 seconds, but at a random time between 0 and 4 seconds. Since the values ​​are different for each client, the requests are scattered across the time axis. In the previous blog simulation, the jittered approach reduced the number of calls by more than half and finished faster than the no-jitter backoff. The two graphs in the picture above illustrate this difference.

Retries must have an end. There are limits on the maximum number of attempts and total waiting time, and if they are exceeded, it is treated as an error and notified to the caller. Without a limit, the number of calls will continue to increase the longer the outage lasts. Interactive requests where users are waiting are better off retrying less and giving up quickly, while batch jobs can wait more and wait longer. Azure's retry patterns document also notes that an aggressive retry policy makes an already busy service worse.

stops.value: 5. Only errors that can be retried
stops.body: All errors should not be retried. Errors that may disappear after a while, such as timeout, disconnected, 429, or 503, are eligible for retry, while 400-series errors that result in the same result no matter how many times you send the same request, such as a malformed request or authentication failure, will not be retried. If there is Retry-After in 429 and 503, the specified time takes priority. Additionally, the operation must be idempotent, meaning that the same request can be executed twice so that it can be safely retried. Retry is used for brief faults, and Circuit Breaker takes care of long-lasting faults.

screens.outro: Now that we've established the limits of retries, let's look at Circuit Breaker, which prevents the call itself in the event of a persistent failure.

screens.title: Circuit Breaker: Calls that will fail are not even attempted
screens.lead: The code below is a simplified example of Circuit Breaker. Select a range of lines from the description on the right to read how each state works. This pattern became widely known through Michael Nygard's book Release It!, and Martin Fowler's often cited article summarizing the key concepts.

visual.alt: A state transition diagram in which the three states of Closed, Open, and Half-Open are connected in a ring shape.

notes.note: The state starts with closed and has a list of recent failure times, a threshold, an aggregation period, a timeout, and the number of trial pass requests. If you set the threshold too low, it will open even for transient faults; if you set it too high, it will open only after the fault has spread.
In the Open state, the call itself is not made until the timeout expires and fails immediately. This prevents immediate failures from tying up waiting resources, breaking the propagation of failures.

When the timeout ends, it switches to half-open and only a small number of requests are allowed to pass. This is a step to prevent the recovering service from collapsing again due to a flood of requests.
on_success is called if the call is successful and on_failure is called if it fails. If failure handling is omitted, the number of failures will not be accumulated and the circuit will not be opened.
Old failures that are out of period are discarded and new failures are added. If the failure reaches the threshold or any half-open fails, it becomes open and starts a new timeout.
When a set number of trial requests are successful in half-open, it returns to closed and clears the failure record. Without this return condition, the circuit will remain half-open forever.

screens.outro: Remembering that it has a different purpose from Retry, we will look at reverting multi-step operations next.

screens.title: Saga and Reward Transactions
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the problems Saga solves and the pros and cons of both coordination methods.

visual.alt: Schematic showing Saga's normal flow and reward flow in case of intermediate failure side by side, top to bottom.

tabs.label: why you need it
tabs.body: Because microservices have their own database for each service, it is difficult to guarantee ACID (atomicity, consistency, isolation, and persistence) for operations across multiple services at once. Saga breaks large tasks into a series of local transactions, and when each step is completed, an event or message triggers the next step. Saga started from a concept proposed by Garcia-Molina and Salem in 1987. To solve the problem that long-running transactions hold up database resources for a long time, slowing down short transactions, long tasks are divided into a series of small transactions, so that they are executed mixed with other tasks, and if they do not reach the end, partial execution is corrected with a compensation transaction. Microservice Saga also applies the same structure across multiple services.

tabs.label: compensation transaction
tabs.body: If an intermediate step fails, a compensatory transaction is executed that reverses the effects of previous steps. This revert is different from a DB rollback. This is because each step has already been committed, and other operations may have changed the same data in the meantime. So compensation is not simply restoration, but work that reflects business rules. For example, reversing a payment is a separate task called a refund.

tabs.label: choreography
tabs.body: Events are exchanged between services without a central coordinator. Each local transaction issues a domain event, which triggers local transactions in other services. This is lightweight for simple flows, but as the number of services increases, it becomes difficult to know who is calling whom and there is a risk of circular dependency.

tabs.label: Orchestration
tabs.body: A central coordinator directs all transactions and tells each participant what to do based on events. The coordinator stores and interprets the state of each task and recovers from failures with compensation transactions. Instead of having the advantage of seeing the flow in one place, the coordinator can become a single point of failure.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the retracement, let's take a look at the queue absorbing the load.

ext.title: Garcia-Molina and Salem, Sagas (Princeton CS technical report TR-070-87)

screens.title: Queue-Based Load Leveling and Dead-letter Queue
screens.lead: Select and expand each item to see the problem it solves and the cost. Open them all and compare.

items.title: Queue-based load leveling
items.body: Place a queue between the sender of the request and the service. The sender of the request places a message containing the data required by the service into a queue, and the service retrieves and processes the message at its own speed. Even if the request rate fluctuates, the service works at a steady pace, so spikes in load don't knock it down. Even if the service is temporarily unavailable, the requesting party can continue to queue, thereby increasing availability. The trade-off is that the response does not come immediately and is asynchronous.

items.title: Dead-letter queue (DLQ)
items.body: Messages that repeatedly fail to be processed are moved to the DLQ when they exceed the reprocessing policy (maxReceiveCount of the redrive policy in Amazon SQS). In DLQ, you can examine the exception log and message contents to diagnose the cause, determine whether enough processing time was given to the consumer, fix the cause, and return the message to the original queue with redrive. DLQ preserves and diagnoses failures rather than eliminating them. In a FIFO queue, the order may be broken, so if the order is important, it is not used.

items.title: Workflow Engine (Durable Functions)
items.body: Directly linking queues and functions improves throughput and reliability, but complicates state management and coordination. Durable Functions provide stateful orchestration. fan-out/fan-in is a parallel processing pattern that executes (fan-out) multiple activities simultaneously and merges (fan-in) the results, which does not scale with a single function and reduces the problem of having to start over if something fails midway.

The Anthropic API is capped not only by requests per minute, but also by input tokens and output tokens per minute. Even with a small number of requests, long inputs and long outputs can fill the limit, so if there is a Retry-After in the response, it follows and speeds it up with a queue.
data.notes: Patterns often overlap one another. For example, when calling a model with a message taken from the queue, it passes Circuit Breaker, and messages that ultimately fail are sent to DLQ. A 429 received due to a spending limit has no Retry-After and retry attempts until the limit is lifted will fail, so it must be excluded from the retry list. Additionally, the path to fallback to an alternative model may result in different output format and quality if the model has not been evaluated, so fallback candidates must be evaluated in advance.

screens.outro: Now, let's move on to the case and start by explaining why retry congestion occurs.

screens.title: Explanation 1: Why does retry flooding occur?
screens.lead: This is a situation where 1000 clients retry immediately upon failure while the external model fails. Select the right arrow to compare the results without and with the circuit breaker.

steps.title: Waiting calls hold up resources
steps.body: If the response is delayed due to a failure, the call remains unfinished and the thread and connection are held. As new requests keep coming in, waiting builds up and other functions that use the same resources are also affected.

steps.title: Retries overlap and the load increases again.
steps.body: If 1000 clients retry immediately upon failure, the moment the service tries to recover, it will again experience a large load. In this case, retrying is an action that expects success, but persistent failures only create more of the same failure. So retries require exponential backoff to widen the interval and jitter to spread out the timing. If the server tells you the time to wait with Retry-After, that value takes precedence.

steps.title: When a circuit is opened, load and occupancy are lost.
steps.body: If the circuit breaker is Open, the call fails immediately without touching the model. Since it does not hold up resources, other functions are not affected, and the load on the model is reduced, leaving room for recovery.

steps.title: Cautiously returning from Half-Open
steps.body: When the timeout ends, we pass only a small number of requests to see if it has recovered. If successful, it returns to Closed, and if any failure occurs, it returns to Open again. This is a step to prevent the load from being concentrated on the recovering service at once.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: Retries and circuit breakers work together rather than competing. Retry handles transient faults and Circuit Breaker handles persistent faults. The retry logic should stop retrying when it receives a signal that the circuit is open.

screens.outro: You also need to decide where the blocked request goes.

screens.title: Commentary 2: Where do blocked requests go?
screens.lead: Each route card selection unfolds user experience, data loss risk, and operational costs. Consider which route is right for you depending on the nature of the service.

items.prompt: Path 1: Respond immediately with a fallback response
items.answer: Returns a cached answer or a simple basic phrase immediately. Users won't wait, but your answers may be of lower quality. There is no risk of data loss and operating costs are low. It is suitable for services where immediacy is important, such as chatbots.

items.prompt: Path 2: Queue and process when recovered
items.answer: Requests are not lost and are processed in order when the service recovers. Users receive the results later. You need to manage the retention period and capacity of your queues. It is suitable for tasks that can tolerate delays, such as generating reports.

items.prompt: Path 3: Repeat failure message is sent to DLQ
items.answer: Instead of discarding unprocessed messages, they are stored in DLQ and the cause is investigated. Setting an alarm will help you find out about problems quickly. The cost is the operational burden of having people look into the DLQ and redrive it.

items.prompt: Path 4: Call a different model instead (fallback)
items.answer: While the primary model is blocked, requests are sent to the alternate model to continue responding. Users will not have to wait, but alternative models may have different output formats and quality, as well as different limits and cost structures, if they have not been evaluated. Therefore, we evaluate fallback candidates in advance and send them out at a small rate on a regular basis to check their operation.

items.prompt: Caution: When using DLQ for order-critical tasks
items.answer: Writing DLQs on FIFO queues can break the exact ordering of messages. If the order changes the context, such as a request following the previous request, DLQ should not be used or the order issue should be handled separately.

screens.outro: In the final commentary, we'll look at reverting when an agent calling multiple tools fails.

screens.title: Commentary 3: Reverting an agent calling multiple tools
screens.lead: Let's solve the agent who calls inventory check, payment, and delivery request in order, and the delivery request fails. Select the right arrow to follow the reversal sequence.

steps.title: Identify points of failure
steps.body: The inventory reservation and payment have already been reflected and the delivery request has failed. If the agent stops here, the discrepancy remains: payment made but no delivery. We need to revert previous steps so that we end up with a consistent final state.

steps.title: Prepare reward tasks for each step
steps.body: Steps that have already been reflected, such as payment, require a separate compensation action called a refund rather than a cancellation request. Retracement proceeds backwards. Make a payment refund first and release the inventory reservation. Compensation is not a simple restoration but a business rule, so it is determined by agreement with the service representative.

steps.title: Avoid duplication with idempotency
steps.body: Retries should not reflect the same operation twice. To ensure that the results do not change even if the same request is repeated, a unique identifier is attached to each request, and identifiers that have already been processed are ignored. Likewise for reward operations, running them twice should not result in two refunds.

steps.title: Orchestrator that records state
steps.body: You should have an orchestrator that records the status of each step so you can know where you went and decide where to start back. Workflow engines like Durable Functions are examples of how to provide this stateful orchestration.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: If a tool called by the model changes external state, the call is a Saga. Regardless of the model's inference quality, without rewards, idempotence, and state history, intermediate failures quickly become inconsistencies.

screens.outro: I will group the three cases into one.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Reliability Patterns Required for AI Invocations
screens.lead: We will organize what we have seen so far into one standard.

paragraphs: AI calls also suffer from the same problems as distributed systems, such as delays, partial failures, and load fluctuations. Therefore, rather than creating a new solution, the solution becomes a matter of attaching an already known pattern to the appropriate point.

Circuit Breaker prevents calls from failing and carefully checks for recovery with Half-Open. It has a different purpose from Retry. Retry expects that it will eventually succeed, and Circuit Breaker prevents calls that will fail at all.

Saga and compensation transactions handle intermediate failures in multi-step operations by reverting them. Queue-based load leveling absorbs the load, and a dead-letter queue preserves messages that eventually fail for diagnosis.
Well-Architected principles tell us to look at reliability in balance with other pillars. The impact of devices that increase reliability on cost and response time must also be considered.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Retries are a tool for transient faults, Circuit Breakers are for persistent failures, Saga is for intermediate failures in multi-step operations, and Queues are for load fluctuations.

data.notes: Each pattern solves only one problem. Find out what's failing, whether the failure is temporary or constant, and whether the order is important, then choose a pattern.

glossary.def: This is a pattern that blocks calls that are likely to fail by managing them in Closed, Open, and Half-Open states.

It is a pattern that divides a large task into a series of multiple local transactions and ensures consistency with a compensation transaction that returns already completed steps in accordance with business rules when failure occurs. In a 1987 paper it was proposed to solve the long transaction problem.
This is a pattern that equalizes load fluctuations by placing a queue between the requesting side and the service.
This is a queue that separately stores messages that repeatedly fail to be processed. Used to diagnose cause and redrive.
This is a property in which the results do not change even if the same task is performed multiple times.
Exponential backoff multiplies the retry waiting time every time there is a failure, and jitter adds randomness to the waiting time to disperse the retry times of clients.

misconceptions.myth: The more retries you make, the more stable it becomes.
misconceptions.fact: Retries are effective for temporary faults, but for persistent faults, they increase the load and cause the fault to spread. Retries require exponential backoff, jitter, and count capping, should be applied only to retry-worthy errors, and should also respond to signals that a circuit is open.

misconceptions.myth: Saga is like a database rollback.
misconceptions.fact: Each step in the Saga has already been committed, and other operations may have changed the data. So reversal requires a separate compensation operation that reflects the business rules.

misconceptions.myth: If there is a dead-letter queue, failure will disappear.
misconceptions.fact: DLQ does not eliminate failures, it only preserves them and allows them to be diagnosed. It is not suitable for tasks where order is important as it may break the order.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: AI calls also suffer from the same failure patterns as distributed systems.
Circuit Breaker prevents calls from failing and ensures recovery with Half-Open.
Saga reverts intermediate failures in multi-step operations to a compensating transaction.
Queues and dead-letter queues absorb the load and retain failed messages.
